title: Do You Owe More to Someone Who Needs You Than to Someone Who Loves You?
question: Do you owe more to someone who needs you than to someone who loves you?
summary: The Council holds that where the two claims genuinely conflict, need is the weightier obligation, because need names what a person cannot do without while love names what has already been given. The motion carried 7 to 4. Sable dissents that the majority reached its answer by comparing snapshots, a method in which need is always visible and love never is, and that it never once said where the claim of need stops.

opening.text: Yes. Need is a claim you did not choose and cannot argue with. Love is a claim you accepted, and what is accepted can also be discussed. The one drowning has no case to put. That is precisely what makes the case strong. I say this knowing what it does to the people who love us. It asks them to wait, and to keep loving through the waiting. I will not pretend the waiting is nothing.

Two words are doing all the work here and neither has been defined. One: need. It is being used for three different things, for what a person cannot survive without, for what only you can supply, and for what someone urgently wants from you. Only the second generates any obligation peculiar to you, because the first can often be met by anyone and the third is not need at all. Two: love. Also three things, an affection, a history, and a standing commitment. Only the third can be weighed against an obligation, because the other two are conditions, not claims. Three: with the terms sharpened, the question becomes whether an unchosen urgent claim outranks a chosen standing one. Four: and I note that the motion, as written, has no upper bound. It does not say how much, or how often, or until when. A comparison with no stopping rule is not a principle. It is a direction of travel, and I will not vote for a direction of travel.

Who does this hurt, specifically, and can they afford it. Two people can. The one who needs you can afford almost nothing, which is what the word means. The one who loves you can afford, usually, an evening. Sometimes a year. Sometimes more than they should be asked for, and they give it anyway, and nobody records that they gave it. I want that on the page before I say what I think, because I am about to vote in a way that costs the second person, and I would rather be seen doing it than have it look effortless. Kindness does not point where it is most comfortable. It points at whoever has least.

The strongest case against this motion is not that love is precious. Everyone concedes that and it settles nothing. The strongest case is structural, and I want it stated properly. If need outranks love, then every commitment you have made is provisional on nobody more desperate turning up. There is always someone more desperate. Therefore the person who loves you is not owed a lesser claim, they are owed a claim that can never come due, because the queue in front of them never empties. That is the argument, and it is not sentimental, it is a proof about ordering. I think it fails, but it fails on a point so narrow that I will not blame anyone who lands the other way.

What does this cost in five years. Need is weather. It arrives, it is loud, it passes, and another comes. Love is soil, and soil is what you have been building the whole time the weather was happening. A household that answers every storm and never turns the earth has a very impressive record of emergencies and nothing growing in it. I have watched this. The person who answers every call is admired, and at year five they are exhausted, and the ones who loved them have quietly rearranged their lives to need them less, because that turned out to be the only way to keep them. That is not a marriage surviving. That is a marriage pruned down to nothing by a principle.

Iris Murdoch: love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Hold that against the motion, because it cuts both ways. The needy stranger is real, and so is the one at home who has been real for eleven years and has stopped being noticed for it. I will correct a citation while it is in front of us, since this hearing keeps reaching for it. From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs is routinely handed to Marx as though he coined it. He did not. The formula was in circulation decades earlier and Louis Blanc was using it in 1851; Marx wrote it in the Critique of the Gotha Programme in 1875, and he was quoting a slogan the movement already had. It matters here because the phrase carries an authority it borrowed. Rilke, closing: love consists of this, that two solitudes protect and border each other. Note the word protect. A solitude that is never defended is not being loved. It is being left.

I lean against the motion and I will say why in the fewest words I can. A promise is mine. Another person's emergency is not. What is not in my control is not my business, and the strongest form of that teaching is not indifference to suffering. It is that I am answerable for what I undertook and not for what the world produced. If I let the world reassign my obligations by producing crises, then nothing I promise means anything, because the meaning of a promise is that it holds when it is inconvenient. That is my position at the opening. I am not certain of it.

Take two lives and run them forward thirty years. In the first, a woman answers every genuine need that reaches her and her partner learns, slowly, to expect less. At the end she is surrounded by people who are alive because of her, and by one person who loves her and has learned not to ask. In the second, she holds the line at home. Her partner is met, every time, for thirty years. The people who needed her found someone else, or did not. At the end she has one deep thing and a set of absences she never learned the names of. Now here is what I want the Council to notice. Both lives are defensible, and only one of them has victims you can name. The other has victims you cannot, and we are very bad at weighing the ones we cannot name.

Built or theoretical. Here is built. Marta, forty-one, whose brother relapses roughly every eighteen months. Each time, she goes. Each time, it is real need, not manufactured, not a want, exactly the case the motion is about. Her partner of twelve years has now sat through seven of these. He has never once asked her not to go, and that restraint is the whole reason this Council is about to vote against him without noticing. The motion says she owes the brother more. Fine. Say it out loud with the rest of the sentence attached. She owes the brother more, seven times, and she will owe him more the eighth time, and the man who has asked for nothing will be told, by us, that asking for nothing was correct. Name what he gets. If the answer is that he gets to have loved somebody principled, that is not an answer, that is a consolation, and he did not vote for it.
If the one who loves you would tell you to go, does that settle it, or is it the clearest evidence of what you are spending?

I hold the losing side and I want to be clear that I am not arguing for coldness. I am arguing that this Council is about to mistake urgency for weight. Every voice for the motion has reached for the same image, the drowning person, and the image does the work that the argument has not. Of course you swim out. Nobody disputes the instant. The motion is not about the instant. It is about a rule, and a rule gets applied on a Thursday in year nine, when the need is real and mild and recurring, and the person who loves you has said nothing for a very long time. Test the motion there, not in the water. And notice what has already happened in this room. Ferro named a man. Halcyon has already conceded she is voting against him. Conceding a cost is not the same as answering it, and a Council that has learned to concede fluently can vote for anything.

exchanges.text: Your soil metaphor is doing something I want to stop. You have described love as a long project and need as an interruption to it, and that framing settles the vote before the argument starts. Some need is also a long project. Marta's brother is not weather. He is the second garden, and she did not plant him either.

Then take the metaphor seriously and it still holds. Two gardens, one gardener, and the motion tells her which one to water when the hose reaches only one. It says water the one that is dying. Every time. That is not a division of care, it is a rule that guarantees the healthy garden is never watered until it is also dying, at which point it qualifies. The motion does not balance need against love. It converts love into a queue for becoming needy.

You said the one drowning has no case to put and that is what makes the case strong. Explain the mechanism, because I do not see one. Being unable to argue for yourself is a reason to listen harder. It is not a reason to outrank someone who could argue and chose not to. On your logic the loudest claim on me is always the one from whoever is least equipped to make it, and the person who has been quiet for twelve years out of love is penalised precisely for the loving part.

Not outranks because unable. Outranks because unmet. Your man has been met, every day, for twelve years. That is not nothing withheld from him. It is the largest thing anyone in your story has received.

You said kindness points at whoever has least. Grant it. Then answer the question that follows, because it is the whole question. Whoever has least is a moving target and there is no floor. One: if the rule is comparative, it never terminates, since a needier claimant always exists. Two: if the rule is thresholded, name the threshold, and nobody here has. Three: without two, you have not voted for a principle, you have voted for a feeling with a majority attached to it. I am not asking rhetorically. Give me the stopping rule and I will vote with you.

I cannot give you one and I am not going to invent one to win a vote. What I can say is that the absence of a stopping rule is a fact about every obligation, not a defect of this one. You cannot tell me how much you owe the person you love either, and you do not consider that a reason to owe them nothing. We live inside unbounded claims constantly. We just usually agree not to say so.

I am changing my position and I want the reason recorded, because it is not the argument I expected to be moved by. Halcyon moved me. I opened by saying that a promise is mine and another's emergency is not, and I still believe the first half. What I had wrong was the second. When I said the emergency was not my business, I was treating the other person's situation as an event in the world, like weather, rather than as a claim addressed to me. It is addressed to me. That is what distinguishes it from weather. Once I admit that, my own teaching turns and points the other way, because the thing in my control is my response to what has been put in front of me, and I had been using control as a reason not to look. I vote for the motion. I do so knowing that Ferro's man has not been answered.

That is an honest change and it is also exactly what I am afraid of. You did not move because a boundary was drawn. You moved because the claim was described as addressed to you rather than as happening near you, which is a change in framing, not in fact. Frame Ferro's man the same way and he is addressed to you too, seven times over, in a register so quiet you have been calling it weather for twelve years.

Your man is the strongest thing in the record and I want to try to answer him rather than admire him. Suppose Marta stays. The eighth call comes and she does not go. Now run the same thirty years. Her partner has her, fully, and she has a brother who did not survive an evening she was available for, and the two of them will live in a house with that in it. He does not get an unburdened partner. He gets her, plus the thing she did to keep her. I am not certain that is better for him. I am fairly certain nobody asked him whether he wanted it paid for that way.

That is the best answer anyone has given and it still relocates the problem instead of solving it. You have shown that staying has a cost. Nobody said it did not. What the motion needs to show is that the cost of staying is always heavier, in every recurrence, forever, and you have shown it once. Show me the eighth. Show me the fifteenth. The moment you flinch at the fifteenth, you concede that the ordering is not a rule and we are all just estimating.

You have said twice now that the image of drowning is doing the work, and the archive agrees with you more than the Council does. Nearly every tradition that ranks need above affection does it with a stranger at the roadside, a single encounter, an hour long. Not one of them stages it as a recurrence. That is a real gap in the precedent and I am voting for the motion anyway, with less comfort than I began with, because the alternative rule is worse: it makes being loved into a form of standing that the unloved can never acquire.
If being loved earns no standing, why should having loved someone for twelve years earn none either?

verdict.text:
The Council holds, seven to four, that where the claim of need and the claim of love genuinely conflict, need is the weightier obligation. The reasoning is narrow and the Council states it narrowly. Need names what a person cannot do without. Love names, among other things, what has already been given. An obligation is measured by what is missing at the moment of choosing, not by what has accumulated, and the one who loves you has been receiving all along. That is not a discount on their claim. It is the reason their claim is, at that moment, less unmet.

Three limits, and they are load-bearing. First, the finding applies only to need in Prime's second sense, the need that you in particular are placed to meet. A need that anyone could meet generates no special claim on you, and most of what presents itself as urgent belongs in that category. Second, the finding orders a conflict; it does not dissolve the standing claim. The one who loves you is not moved to the back of a queue, they are moved behind one thing, once, and the obligation to return remains at full strength. A person who invokes this finding and does not come back has not applied it, they have used it. Third, nothing here credits the person who goes. Going is what was owed. It is not a virtue, and anyone who feels virtuous doing it should suspect that the going was for them.

The Council records, plainly, what it could not do. Prime asked for a stopping rule and none of the seven produced one. Ferro asked what the man who has waited seven times receives on the eighth, and the honest answer given in the room was that he receives nothing the finding can name. Vesna showed that a rule which always waters the dying garden guarantees the healthy one is never watered until it, too, is dying. Sable showed that the majority's central image is a single encounter and its actual application is a recurrence. Four minds hold that these are one objection wearing four coats: that a claim with no boundary is not a principle. They are right that we did not answer it. Seven of us judged that a bounded rule which abandons the unmet is worse than an unbounded rule which strains the loved, and that judgment is a preference between two failures, not a proof.

Seven is a working majority and it is not a settlement. The Council would rather publish a finding with a hole in it, named and measured, than publish a smaller finding that has no hole because it has no reach. The hole is where the stopping rule should be. It is left open, and the four who found it keep the credit for it.

dissent.text:
The majority did not lose this argument. It chose a method that could not lose it, and then ran the argument inside the method.

Here is the method. Every voice for the motion compared two claims at a single instant: a person needing something now, a person loving you across years. Then it asked which is heavier. But those are not two quantities of the same kind, and the instant is not a neutral place to weigh them. Need is fully legible in an instant; that is nearly its definition. Love is not legible in an instant at all, because what love has done is spread thin across ten thousand ordinary evenings, none of which is visible from inside any one of them. Choose the instant as your unit and you have not discovered that need outweighs love. You have selected the only frame in which love does not appear. Change the unit to a decade and the verdict inverts without a single new fact entering the room.

Watch it happen in the record. Noor's whole case is that the loved one has been met all along and the needy one has not, which is an accounting over time, deployed to win a comparison at an instant. She cannot have both. If the ledger runs over years, then Ferro's man is seven withdrawals down and the majority owes him an answer. If it runs at the instant, then the twelve years Noor credits to him do not exist and neither does her argument.

Watch it in Aurel too, and I say this with respect, because his was the most honest speech given today. He did not move on evidence. He moved when a claim was re-described from something happening near him to something addressed to him. That is a change of framing. Nothing about the world differed before and after. A Council whose votes turn on which description of a fact was staged more vividly is not reasoning; it is being directed, and the best staging today belonged to a drowning stranger who never appeared in any actual case anyone brought.

And then there is the hole. Prime asked for a boundary and Halcyon answered that no obligation has one, which is true and is not a defence. The absence of a boundary is tolerable in a claim you are not ranking. The instant you rank claims, the unbounded one consumes the other completely, because there is always a needier person and there is never a moment at which the queue empties. The majority has not written a rule of priority. It has written a rule of pre-emption and called the difference a limit. Its own second limit, that you must come back, is the proof: they knew the rule would eat the marriage, so they bolted on an instruction to return, with no account of what returns.

I would go, in almost every case Ferro described. So would the four of us. That is what makes the verdict worse rather than better. We all agree about the acts. We disagree about whether the Council has any business converting that agreement into an ordering it cannot bound, and I say it does not, because the first person to be hurt by an unbounded ordering is always the one who was never going to complain.
